title: Could There Be A Loch Ness Monster?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Loch Ness Monster legend: the formation of Loch Ness by glacial action about ten thousand years ago, early legends including Pictish carvings and St. Columba's reported encounter, the 1933 surge of sightings and the Daily Mail hiring Marmaduke Wetherell, who was humiliated by the hippo-foot tracks hoax. They cover Constance Whyte's 1957 book More Than a Legend, 1960s-70s sonar and underwater photography expeditions (Robert Rines, Harold Edgerton, Peter Scott and the name Nessiteras rhombopteryx), the 1987 Operation Deep Scan, the 1990s Urquhart Castle project, the 2006 Norwegian sonar find that turned out to be a prop from The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes, the 1934 Surgeon's Photo and its later exposure as a hoax by Alistair Boyd, skeptical explanations such as Wels catfish, swimming circus elephants, plesiosaurs and sauropods, and a 2018 environmental DNA survey. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about Cooperative for Education (CoEd) sponsorship of girls' education in Guatemala.

entities.name: The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter, note that Loch Ness was touched on in an earlier sea monsters episode, and set up the episode's timeline.

segments.title: Formation of Loch Ness and its geography
segments.summary: Loch Ness was gouged by an ice sheet and filled by melting glacier about ten thousand years ago. It is long, deep, and dark from peat runoff. The hosts compare it to lakes in Georgia, which are mostly man-made.

segments.title: Pictish carvings and early legends
segments.summary: The Picts carved stones with animal images, including one that may depict a Loch Ness-like creature. Water kelpie legends and St. Columba's reported encounter with a monster in the 560s are described.

segments.title: 1933 sightings and the Daily Mail
segments.summary: Road construction in 1933 gave more access to the loch. The McKay sighting in April 1933 led to the word monster being used. Sightings surged, and the King Kong release is mentioned as a factor. The Daily Mail sent Marmaduke Wetherell to investigate in December.

segments.title: Hippo footprint hoax
segments.summary: Wetherell found tracks he estimated came from a creature at least twenty feet long. Museum experts later identified the prints as from a taxidermied hippo foot. Wetherell was humiliated, and interest in Nessie waned for decades.

segments.title: Eyewitnesses and Constance Whyte's book
segments.summary: Thousands of people reported sightings, including a Nobel laureate and other respectable witnesses. Dr Constance Whyte collected accounts and published More Than a Legend in 1957, which gave the subject scientific interest.

segments.title: Sonar expeditions and Robert Rines photographs
segments.summary: Expeditions from Oxford, Cambridge, Birmingham and the BBC used sonar in the 1960s and 70s. Tim Dinsdale filmed something in 1960s. Robert Rines combined side scan sonar with underwater photography in 1975, and Harold Edgerton and Peter Scott supported the work. Rines presented evidence to the House of Commons.

segments.title: Nessiteras rhombopteryx name and Peter Scott's plesiosaur claim
segments.summary: Scott and Rines published a paper in Nature giving the monster the scientific name Nessiteras rhombopteryx, partly to satisfy a conservation law requiring a binomial name. Scott called it a plesiosaur. The hosts note the anagram 'monster hoax by Sir Peter S.' and Scott's denial.

segments.title: Operation Deep Scan and Urquhart Castle project
segments.summary: Operation Deep Scan in 1987 used twenty-four boats with side scan sonar to search the loch and found three unexplained large moving targets. The early 1990s Urquhart Castle project, led by Nicholas Witchell, studied biology and geology and recorded another unexplained moving mass.

segments.title: 2006 Norwegian sonar find and Sherlock Holmes prop
segments.summary: A 2006 Norwegian expedition sonar image showed a large object on the lake bottom. It turned out to be a prop from the 1970 film The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes.

segments.title: Surgeon's Photo and the hoax exposure
segments.summary: The 1934 Surgeon's Photo, attributed to London surgeon Kenneth Wilson, became the famous Nessie image. A 1984 analysis suggested a bird or otter. Alistair Boyd later investigated and concluded it was a hoax, with Christian Spurling confessing to a model built on a toy submarine as revenge against the Daily Mail.

segments.title: Skeptical explanations: catfish, elephants, plesiosaurs and sauropods
segments.summary: Steve Feltham proposed a giant Wels catfish. Another explanation is swimming circus elephants. The hosts argue that plesiosaurs and sauropods would need to breathe air often, the loch is too small to support a breeding population, and no bones or remains have been found.

segments.title: Environmental DNA survey and protection law
segments.summary: In 2018 researchers collected environmental DNA samples from the loch, yielding about five million sequences that are being analyzed. A protective order would apply to any new species found there. The hosts mention the film Incident at Loch Ness.

segments.title: Listener mail: CoEd Guatemala
segments.summary: The hosts promote Cooperative for Education (CoEd), which aims to keep eight thousand girls in Guatemala in school, and describe student sponsorship options.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information and sign off.
